blocks.text: The working prototype runs the child-facing game, manages three-player turns and holds the current game state. The wider concept adds saved individual records and a Teacher App; these were not connected to the final electronics prototype.

items.title: What the visit examined
items.body: Could participants follow a turn, choose a physical answer and understand the game’s feedback with teacher support? The trial exposed instructions, screen visibility and sensor problems in that loop.

items.title: What remains a proposal
items.body: Helping educators compare independent answers, hints and support across sessions requires saved records and a connected teacher view. The classroom visit did not evaluate that wider service.

blocks.text: A correct answer alone does not tell an educator how a child reached it: independently, after several attempts or with a hint. Our design challenge was to make communication, emotion and shape practice clear and hands-on for autistic learners, while giving educators a way to understand the support behind each answer. We framed this challenge through secondary research.

items.title: For the learner
items.body: Show a clear prompt, offer physical answer choices and give predictable feedback, allowing for different response speeds and support needs.

items.title: For the educator
items.body: Understand attempts, time and support without having to write down every response while helping with the activity.

items.title: Our direction
items.body: Connect physical play to a simple phone interface, with a proposed record of how each answer was reached.

blocks.text: We treated communication, emotion recognition and shape interaction as practice activities. The game is not a diagnostic or therapeutic assessment. Its intended learning value still needs evaluation beyond one visit.

The questions and answer cards pair pictures with short English text. We therefore selected participants who could read independently for the field trial. Use by learners who cannot yet read remains untested.
Final documentation: background and problem framing, pages 5–10; scope, page 26; participant selection, page 33.

We explored three ways to answer physically: place an emotion token, arrange routine cards, or connect a situation with an emotion and response. We used SCAMPER, a set of prompts for changing an existing idea, to question the board, answer objects, feedback and progression while refining Giggles.

Present a short situation, then place the corresponding emotion token on a base. This direction explored a star light, a celebration after five stars and progression towards more complex emotions and responses.

blocks.text: The alternatives separated three kinds of practice: recognising an emotion, ordering a routine and choosing a response to a situation. Giggles brought communication, emotion and shape activities into one board. That meant the questions could change while players kept the same turn sequence and physical-answer rule.

The phone presents the question, but the answer happens on the board. For Communication and Emotion, the player chooses a card and taps it on the reader. For Shapes, the player presses a matching physical shape. This keeps the same question-and-answer sequence across the three activities.

blocks.text: Testing showed that this split was not always clear: participants tried to answer on the phone screen. We proposed reader lights, an arrow and spoken guidance to make the answer location easier to find.

The documented bank contains six prompts per category. Four Communication cards and four Emotion cards can answer several situations; each question also has a stored hint. These are the defined activity responses, not recorded participant results.

blocks.text: Emotion matches are simplified expectations inside the game. They are not universal rules about how someone must feel, and matching a card does not demonstrate real-world emotional understanding.

The full question bank contains Triangle and Star prompts, while the final firmware implements Circle and Square answer controls. The documentation does not identify whether those unsupported prompts were excluded from the active build. The tables show the intended content, not proof that all six Shape prompts were playable. Before another session, the active question list must be matched to its physical answers; completing the physical shape set remains future development.

I programmed three levels of support: Try Again, a question-specific hint, then the answer. The same question stays active until the player gives the correct physical response, even after the answer is shown. This lets the player finish the action instead of being moved on immediately after a mistake.

blocks.caption: Feedback and turn progression

Reveal the answer; still wait for the correct physical response.
Green feedback, positive speech and a score increment, then advance the turn.
Give positive feedback and advance, without the same pre-reveal point.

blocks.text: The third wrong response does not force a new question. The child still supplies the correct card or implemented shape press before the next turn. A pre-reveal score can follow a hint, so it is not a measure of first-attempt correctness.

blocks.text: I used an ESP32, a small programmable controller, to connect the card reader, sensors, shape buttons, feedback lights and phone interface. The RC522 reader identifies each RFID card. The phone connects over local Wi-Fi, so the working game does not need a separate computer or cloud server.
Physical event → game state → feedback

items.title: Read the input
items.body: A category sensor, RFID card or shape control supplies the physical event.

items.title: Apply the rules
items.body: The ESP32 chooses the question, checks the answer and coordinates feedback and turns.

items.title: Present the state
items.body: The phone reads the current game data from /state, updates the screen and speaks the prompt or feedback.

blocks.text: This split gives each part one job: the controller decides which answers and inputs are valid, while the phone presents the current state. For example, a Shape question accepts a physical shape press and ignores an RFID answer; the replay card is accepted only after the whole game ends.
Build and integrate

We tested controller inputs separately, verified RFID identifiers and LED responses, then connected the interaction logic to the phone. This helped separate electrical, firmware and browser faults. The main loop keeps input handling, delayed advance, finish handling and web requests in separate functions.

blocks.text: I wrote the controller program in Arduino C++, using WiFi, WebServer, SPI, MFRC522 and LittleFS. SPI is the connection to the card reader; LittleFS stores the images on the controller. The phone reads JSON game data from /state and images from /img/. The controller checks answers and turns; the browser displays and speaks the result.

blocks.caption: Five states keep inputs in context
rows: Wait for the active player’s category or finish input.
Enable the appropriate physical answer input.
Show individual completion for five seconds.
Show final completion and accept the replay card.

blocks.text: The report describes six questions per category with separate used-question tracking: select from the available pool and reset after all six are used. It does not provide a versioned active question list to reconcile the six Shape prompts with the two implemented controls. The firmware cycles through three players. It does not establish automated dice reading or separate pawn detection on all 18 learning blocks.

visuals.alt: A working notebook page with sensor, button and RFID-to-ESP32 pin assignments. Some assignments differ from the final firmware.
visuals.caption: Working wiring notes · The notebook differs from the final firmware; the table below records the final connections.

blocks.text: Shape buttons use internal pull-ups and read LOW when pressed; category and finish inputs are active HIGH. The circuit shares a common ground. Debounce timers reduce repeated input counts, although the field trial exposed a different problem: intentional finger-counting could trigger a category before the pawn arrived.
Replay is accepted only at final completion. The card clears in-session data and returns to Start; it is ignored during normal play so a stray tap cannot restart the session.
Final documentation, pages 26–32. Its functional checklist has blank result cells; the checklist is not a completed pass report.

blocks.text: Compare each child primarily with their own history. Response speed, retries and hints need an educator’s context; they should not diagnose, rank or define a child’s ability.

We tested Giggles with four participants at Vishwansh Foundation, Pune: one adult aged 24 individually, and three children aged 8–10 in a group game. We first explained the board, cards, shape buttons and a complete turn to the teachers. They then introduced and supported play using their familiar classroom approach.

rows: A full three-player game facilitated by teachers.

blocks.text: Participants were selected because they could read independently. Each participant played one session during a single visit, with teachers introducing and supporting both formats.

blocks.text: Use the classroom’s existing routines

Before play, the teacher wrote each player’s pawn colour on the whiteboard. This reused the class’s familiar place for instructions and reminders, giving players a visible reference for their pawn. Teachers supported the first one or two attempts as participants learned where to tap, press and choose.

blocks.caption: What happened during play
columns: What it means for the next build
rows: Children read questions and options aloud, chose a card and tapped the reader.
Teachers guided reading and the first one or two attempts. LEDs, audio and the phone responded to physical answers.
Preserve the physical answer and feedback loop; add a practice turn and reader cues so instructions arrive before the action.
Three players needed to see a screen facing one side.
The board had to be rotated each turn so the next child could see it.
Try a shared-screen arrangement. Check visibility from each seat without moving the board.
Children forgot their pawn or counted from Start; counting fingers also activated questions early.
The whiteboard kept pawn colours visible, but did not resolve turn and counting confusion. Touch sensors could respond before the pawn arrived.
Repeat player colour at the point of play and distinguish counting from arrival before recording question timing.

blocks.text: These are summaries from the final report, not reconstructed individual session logs. Matching and pressing the shapes was reported as particularly engaging. Teacher guidance is part of this evidence: a completed answer does not establish that it was independent.
Final documentation: session setup and observations, pages 33–35; evidence limits, page 41. No structured task-success rate or longitudinal learning measure is reported.

The sessions revealed eight pain points, from learning the rules to seeing the shared screen and triggering questions too early. Each observation below is paired with a proposed change for the next version. These changes have not been implemented and retested in the documented work.

blocks.before: Children needed help during the first one or two attempts: where to tap, which shape to press and which card to choose. Once the flow became familiar, they enjoyed playing.
blocks.after: Guide the next action at the board with a glowing reader zone, lit shape controls and an on-screen picture of what to use.

blocks.beforeTitle: Rules arrived after play had started
blocks.before: Without a practice round, children had to learn the rules and play at the same time, which caused confusion.
blocks.after: Add a short demonstration round that walks through one practice turn with audio before the real game begins.

blocks.beforeTitle: Two card categories looked like one set
blocks.before: Emotion and situation cards were confused when the decks sat beside one another.
blocks.after: Give each category a consistent colour and symbol across card, tray and screen, such as a speech bubble for situations and a face for emotions.

blocks.before: The prototype had no Hindi or Marathi option for either the on-screen text or spoken prompts.
blocks.after: Add Hindi and Marathi text and audio, with a per-child language choice in the proposed Teacher App.

blocks.beforeTitle: Only one side could see the screen
blocks.before: With three players around the board, the screen faced one side. The board had to be rotated each turn so the next child could see it.
blocks.after: Explore a raised, rotating screen stand in the centre, or mirrored displays that every player can see.

blocks.beforeTitle: Pawn ownership and counting were unclear
blocks.before: Children forgot which pawn was theirs and sometimes counted from Start instead of their current position.
blocks.after: Repeat each player’s pawn colour on screen and illuminate the occupied block as the starting point for counting.

blocks.beforeTitle: The display looked like the answer surface
blocks.before: Children tried to touch the phone screen to answer instead of tapping their card on the RFID reader.
blocks.after: Point to the reader with an on-screen arrow, a spoken “Tap your card here” cue and a light on the reader itself.

blocks.before: Touching blocks while counting activated a question before the pawn reached its destination.
blocks.after: Explore detection that responds only to the pawn, such as a magnet or tag, or show the counting hops on screen.

blocks.text: Final documentation: eight pain-point cards on pages 37–38, introduced as proposed next-round fixes on page 36.
The documentation identifies ten strengths to retain. These combine observed reactions with useful design qualities; they are not ten measured learning outcomes.

items.title: One question at a time
items.body: Each screen keeps one picture and one question in focus.

items.title: A consistent layout
items.body: Communication, Emotion and Shape questions use the same screen structure, so the next prompt has a familiar place.

items.title: Support before completion
items.body: Try Again, then a hint and answer reveal, keeps another attempt available instead of ending the turn with a punitive message.

items.title: An answer they can hold or press
items.body: Physical cards and buttons turn the response into a tap or press rather than another screen control.

items.title: Audio alongside the question
items.body: A speaker option reads the question aloud. The documented participants could read independently; use by non-readers was not tested.

items.title: A calm visual base
items.body: Cream backgrounds, rounded forms and soft colour are design choices to retain while refining the interaction.

items.title: A familiar educator nearby
items.body: Teachers introduced and supported play in their familiar classroom manner. Connected app monitoring remains a future feature.

items.title: Familiar situations
items.body: Lunch boxes, shoelaces, gifts and sharing gave communication questions an everyday context.

items.title: Shapes invited a physical response
items.body: Finding and pressing the matching shape was a particularly engaging part of the session.

items.title: Requests to play again
items.body: The documentation records children asking for another round after the game ended—a qualitative sign of interest.

blocks.text: The useful pattern was engagement after teacher guidance, especially around physical responses, with requests to play again. We would preserve those parts while making the first turns clearer. These observations do not establish gains in reading, motor skills, real-world transfer or retention.
Final documentation: six strengths on page 40 and four continuing at the top of page 41.

I would fix the instructions, shared-screen visibility and premature sensor activation before adding more metrics. If a question starts while a child is still counting, its timing and attempts would be hard to interpret. The next build should make the intended turn reliable, then be retested over several sessions before connecting saved records and the Teacher App.

blocks.caption: A proposed build order for the eight findings
columns: What to observe after the change
rows: Compare pawn-only detection with an explicit arrival action. First reconcile active Shape prompts with the controls actually available; neither fix is complete.
Count and move a pawn without starting a question early; then finish the intended answer and next turn. Check every active Shape prompt has a valid physical response.
2 · First-use guidance, missing practice round, mixed card decks and touchscreen expectations.
Build one practice turn, consistent category symbols and a visible reader cue. Keep the answer on the board while making that location clear on screen.
Where does the learner try to answer? Record the teacher’s prompt, the learner’s action and the game response, including help still needed.
Compare a central rotating stand with mirrored displays; repeat pawn colour and current position near the turn. These remain alternatives to try, not a selected tested solution.
Can each player see the prompt and start counting from the current position without rotating the whole board?
Review the prompts and hints with educators before adding Hindi and Marathi. Define text, speech and support needs together, then test the chosen language flow.
Can the intended learner understand the instruction and answer options with their usual support? Keep outside help distinct from software hints.

items.title: Test the next build over time
items.body: Run another round with more participants and several sessions. Record support, attempts, response time, hint use and sensor behaviour, while keeping teacher facilitation visible in the evidence.

items.title: Then connect the educator system
items.body: Persist a real session record before extending the dashboard or AI summaries. Review with educators whether attempts, hints and separately recorded teacher help explain the answer; do not treat a pre-reveal score as independent success.

blocks.text: What this visit can support

Four participants and one visit give us issues to investigate, rather than evidence of a lasting learning benefit. Teachers helped participants, and early hardware caused some breakdowns. We have not measured learning, retention, changes in engagement over time or the effect of the proposed fixes.

The next version should keep one question at a time, a consistent layout, supportive feedback, audio and tangible shape interaction. The aim is to reduce avoidable setup and turn friction without removing the teacher’s role.

Giggles received Best Project at Meraki, our pre-grad show. My main contribution was connecting the physical inputs, game rules and phone feedback into a working prototype. The classroom trial then showed what that working system still needed: clearer instructions and better support for shared play.

visual.alt: Lakshya holding the Giggles certificate and award in front of the Meraki project display.
visual.caption: Giggles received Best Project at Meraki, our pre-grad show.

items.title: An input needs the right meaning
items.body: Debouncing filters repeated electrical signals. It does not distinguish a counting finger from a pawn. That requires a different sensing decision, not just another timer.

items.title: Physical controls still need guidance
items.body: A functioning reader or button is not enough if a player expects a touchscreen or mixes the card decks. The next action needs to be clear where the player is looking.

items.title: Shared play changes the requirements
items.body: A phone that is readable from one seat is not equally visible to three players. Screen position, pawn colour and counting cues need to work around the whole board.

story.intro: Giggles is a learning board game for autistic children. A phone shows each question; players answer by tapping a card on the reader or pressing a physical shape. I built the electronics, game logic and working prototype during the six-week project; teammates designed the interfaces, which I helped review. Testing at Vishwansh Foundation showed where the instructions, shared screen and turns needed to be clearer.

outcome.title: Current outcome
outcome.text: A working physical–digital game and a teacher-supported trial with four participants. The visit identified eight interaction issues and ten strengths to carry forward. The Teacher App and post-test fixes remain proposed; learning gains have not been measured.
